lesson.title: Where Rational Functions Break: Continuity Away from the Zeros
lesson.summary: A rational function is continuous everywhere except where its denominator equals zero, and whether that break is a removable hole or an infinite discontinuity depends on whether the numerator vanishes there too.
lesson.body:
A rational function is a quotient of two polynomials, f(x) = p(x)/q(x), and since polynomials are continuous everywhere, you might expect rational functions to inherit that good behavior almost automatically. They do, with exactly one caveat: division by zero is never allowed, so a rational function cannot be continuous, or even defined, at any point where its denominator equals zero. Everywhere else, continuity carries over directly from the polynomials that make it up.

The precise tool here is the quotient law for continuity: if f and g are both continuous at a point a, and g(a) is not zero, then f/g is also continuous at a. Since every polynomial is continuous at every real number, this law immediately tells you that p(x)/q(x) is continuous at every a for which q(a) is not zero. So the domain of continuity for a rational function is simply the set of real numbers left over after removing the zeros of the denominator.

At the zeros of q(x), the story splits into two distinct cases, both examples of discontinuity. If the same factor that makes q(a) = 0 also makes p(a) = 0, the two functions share a common factor that can be canceled algebraically, and the discontinuity is removable: the limit exists, but the function value does not, so the graph shows a single missing point, a hole. If instead p(a) is not zero while q(a) is zero, no cancellation is possible, and the function's values grow without bound near a, producing an infinite discontinuity rather than a removable one.

Consider f(x) = (x^2 - 1)/(x - 1). Factoring the numerator gives (x - 1)(x + 1)/(x - 1), which simplifies to x + 1 for every x except x = 1, where the original expression is 0/0 and therefore undefined. Even though f(1) does not exist, the limit as x approaches 1 does exist, since the simplified form x + 1 gives 1 + 1 = 2. So f has a removable discontinuity at x = 1, a hole in the graph at the point (1, 2), while it agrees with the continuous polynomial x + 1 everywhere else and is continuous at every other real number.

Now contrast that with g(x) = (x + 1)/(x - 1). At x = 1 the denominator is again zero, but the numerator is 1 + 1 = 2, which is not zero, so no cancellation is possible. Checking values near x = 1 shows what happens: at x = 1.1, g(1.1) = 2.1/0.1 = 21, and at x = 0.9, g(0.9) = 1.9/(-0.1) = -19. As x approaches 1 from the right the values grow toward positive infinity, and from the left they plunge toward negative infinity. This is an infinite discontinuity, not a hole, and it corresponds to a vertical asymptote at x = 1, a feature explored in detail shortly.

The general strategy for describing continuity of any rational function is therefore: factor numerator and denominator completely, cancel any common factors, and note that the function is continuous everywhere except at the zeros of the original, unsimplified denominator. Canceled zeros become removable holes, while uncanceled zeros become infinite discontinuities. This factor-and-classify approach will reappear whenever you need to sketch a rational function's graph or evaluate a limit that initially looks like 0/0.
